cells.tense: You are reading the shape of things and steering by it, right here, with your hand in it.
cells.act: make something skilled and small on the cleared ground
cells.ask: Something you noticed this week — the way it actually works. Build a small version of it one evening, small enough to hold up and show somebody. It only has to exist.
cells.core:
You can see how something works before anyone has said it, and these days that doesn't just sit in you. Somebody's stuck in a mess of particulars and you name the shape they're standing in, and it lands, because the shape was really there. Then you show the way across.

Seeing through things has a cost. You can also see where it all goes wrong three steps out, and that can start to feel like it's already been done. So take what you noticed and build it — a small version, one evening, something you can hold up and show. It doesn't have to matter. It needs to be outside your head, where it can be looked at.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the shape and show the way across.
cells.verb: Chart passage through the pattern, carrying others across.
cells.place: In pure pattern, where shape shows and content is gone.

cells.tense: You will be standing at the far side already, having chosen the route they cannot see yet.
cells.act: engage the hard part on purpose and see what holds
cells.ask: Name the piece of this you've been routing around. Go straight at it for one stretch of one day, and stop once your methods have shown which of them survive.
cells.core:
You can see the far side from here, and the people you're going with haven't started walking. So you lay it out for them — the route, the turns, the wrong one they'd have taken — and you keep laying it out, because it's going to happen any day now and they'll need it. The plan on the table keeps getting longer. It gets confirmed from here over and over, which isn't the same as walked.

Something is ready to be let go. A plan stops needing to be tested once part of it has been tried for real. So take the hard piece you've been going around and spend a stretch of one day on it, long enough to find out which of your methods was only true on paper. What's left standing is what you were really offering.

cells.tense: You had the shape in your hand and you have been looking back at it while the door shut behind you.
cells.act: let the inner compass decide the small case
cells.ask: Find the smallest matter still sitting open, the kind that looks like yours to settle. Decide it alone, tell nobody, then leave it where it lies.
cells.core:
You know how things pass from one person to another, and you've gone quiet in the place where that knowing would be worth something. You see what a stuck person needs and you say nothing, because saying it feels like steering, and you're not sure steering is yours. It stops at your hand.

What has come back instead is a small sense of what's fair and what's owed — something that belongs to you to settle. Start at the smallest case, not the loudest. Decide it alone, with no one watching and no one told afterward. A mind that charts passage gets its energy back from doing the fair small thing it sees, and from nothing else.

cells.tense: You are reading the shape of things and filing it under the way things happen to go.
cells.act: let the vision be shared with one other
cells.ask: You saw how something worked. Sit down with somebody and lay out the real version of it, not the summary, so that both of you are looking at the same thing.
cells.core:
The direction comes out of you and you don't put your name on it. You say the useful thing and count it as being useful; you name the shape and it's just what was there. The reading of the pattern is happening in you — it is you doing it — and asked, you'd shrug and say the situation made the call, or that you were passing along what anyone could see.

But that habit was borrowed from an earlier, plainer form of the same thing: not standing alone with a chart, but meeting somebody and walking the same way. So take a piece of the pattern and sit down with a person, not to advise them — to look at the same thing together. What gets looked at that way tends to stay put, and your hand is in it where you can see it.
